definition: Light sent back from a surface. Physically, it is the backward wave radiated in step by electrons that the incoming light drives at a boundary.
Light passing through a material. The transmitted wave is the incoming wave plus the forward waves re-radiated by the material's driven electrons.
Removal of light energy by a material, usually ending up as heat; it happens when the light's frequency matches a natural frequency (an energy gap) of the material's electrons or bonds.
Redirection of light into many directions by small particles, pores, boundaries, or density fluctuations; it is counted as diffuse reflection or diffuse transmission.
The constant α in I = I₀e^(−αx), in m⁻¹; after a depth of 1/α, about 37% of the light remains.
Mirror-like reflection from a surface whose bumps are much smaller than the wavelength, so parallel rays stay parallel and an image survives.
Reflection from a rough surface (bumps comparable to the wavelength or larger); each ray obeys the law of reflection locally, but rays leave in all directions.
Radiation from electrons forced to oscillate by a light wave, at the same frequency and with a fixed phase relationship to it; the basis of reflection and refraction.
The frequency below which a metal's free electrons can follow an EM wave and reflect it; for most metals it lies in the ultraviolet, and above it the metal becomes transparent.
The thin surface layer (tens of nanometers for visible light in metals) within which a metal cancels and absorbs an incoming EM wave.
The ratio n = c/v of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of wave crests in a material; it also gives the factor by which the wavelength shrinks.
The rule n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ for how much light bends when it crosses a boundary between materials, with angles measured from the normal.
The angle of incidence, given by sin θc = n₂/n₁, beyond which light traveling from a higher-index to a lower-index material cannot escape.
Complete (100%) reflection of light inside a higher-index material when it strikes the boundary beyond the critical angle; it guides light in optical fibers.
A thin glass core surrounded by lower-index cladding that guides light over long distances by repeated total internal reflection.
The dependence of refractive index on wavelength; in glass and water n is larger for violet than for red, which separates colors in prisms and rainbows.
The distance from a lens to the point where it brings parallel rays to a focus (converging lens) or from which they appear to diverge (diverging lens).
The unit of lens power, P = 1/f with f in meters; the human eye has roughly 60 diopters, about two-thirds of it from the cornea.
A direction-dependent refractive index found in non-cubic crystals such as quartz, calcite, and sapphire; it makes grain boundaries in polycrystalline ceramics scatter light.
Letting light through only diffusely, so objects behind cannot be seen clearly; caused by internal scattering, as in dense polycrystalline alumina.
